cls: Beta-blocker - cardioselective (beta-1) with beta-2 agonist and vasodilator activity
pharm: Selectively blocks beta-1 adrenoceptors while exerting partial beta-2 agonist and mild vasodilator activity, lowering blood pressure and heart rate with relatively little effect on airways and peripheral resistance

summary: Celiprolol is a cardioselective (beta-1 selective) beta-blocker that also has partial beta-2 agonist activity and mild peripheral vasodilator action, used mainly to treat hypertension. The usual dose is 200 mg once daily taken before food, increased to 400 mg once daily if the response is inadequate. Because absorption is reduced by food, dosing should be consistent on an empty stomach. As with other beta-blockers, it can cause bradycardia, fatigue, dizziness and should be used cautiously in heart failure, conduction disorders, asthma/COPD, diabetes and peripheral vascular disease, and not stopped abruptly. Its relative beta-1 selectivity and vasodilator profile mean it tends to have less effect on airways and peripheral circulation than non-selective agents.

admin: Take once daily in the morning before food (food markedly reduces absorption)
Swallow tablets with water; keep timing relative to meals consistent
Do not stop treatment abruptly - taper to avoid rebound hypertension, angina or arrhythmia

moa: Celiprolol selectively antagonises beta-1 adrenoceptors in the heart, reducing heart rate, myocardial contractility and renin release, which lowers blood pressure. Unlike many beta-blockers it also has partial agonist (intrinsic sympathomimetic) activity at beta-2 receptors and a mild direct vasodilator effect, which tend to reduce peripheral vascular resistance and limit bronchoconstriction and adverse metabolic effects. The net result is reduced cardiac workload and blood pressure with a comparatively favourable peripheral and respiratory profile.

absolute: Second- or third-degree AV block (without a pacemaker)
Marked sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome
relative: Asthma or chronic obstructive airways disease

preg: Beta-blockers, including celiprolol, cross the placenta and may cause fetal and neonatal bradycardia, hypoglycaemia and intrauterine growth restriction. Use during pregnancy should be avoided unless clearly necessary, at the lowest effective dose, with monitoring of the neonate after delivery.
lact: Beta-blockers are excreted into breast milk. Celiprolol should be used with caution during breastfeeding, and the infant should be observed for signs of beta-blockade such as bradycardia or hypoglycaemia.
renal: Celiprolol is partly eliminated by the kidneys, so accumulation can occur in renal impairment. Reduce the dose in patients with significant renal impairment and titrate cautiously while monitoring heart rate and blood pressure.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; consider lower doses and monitor response, as altered metabolism may affect drug levels and tolerability.

major: Verapamil or diltiazem (rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers) - additive bradycardia, AV block and hypotension; avoid combination especially IV
Other antiarrhythmics and amiodarone - additive cardiac depression and conduction slowing
Clonidine - risk of rebound hypertension if clonidine is stopped while on a beta-blocker
moderate: Insulin and oral hypoglycaemics - may mask hypoglycaemia symptoms and prolong recovery
NSAIDs - may blunt the antihypertensive effect
Sympathomimetics and adrenaline - altered pressor response
minor: Digoxin - additive effects on AV conduction
interactions.food: Food significantly reduces celiprolol absorption - take before meals on an empty stomach
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may enhance the blood-pressure-lowering effect; use moderately
interactions.diagnostics: May mask tachycardia from hypoglycaemia or hyperthyroidism; can affect catecholamine-based diagnostic tests

rare: Sleep disturbance, depression or mood changes
Worsening of peripheral vascular disease or psoriasis
emergency: Symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade AV block
Acute decompensated heart failure or severe hypotension

monitoring: Blood pressure and heart rate during titration and follow-up
Signs and symptoms of heart failure
Respiratory function in patients with airways disease
Blood glucose in patients with diabetes
Peripheral circulation in patients with vascular disease
counsel: Take this tablet once a day in the morning before food, at about the same time each day
Do not stop the medicine suddenly - tell your doctor before stopping, as abrupt withdrawal can worsen heart symptoms
Report breathlessness, swollen ankles, a very slow pulse, fainting or wheezing
If you have diabetes, be aware the medicine can hide some warning signs of low blood sugar
Rise slowly from sitting or lying to reduce dizziness, especially when starting treatment
Tell other prescribers you take a beta-blocker before starting new medicines
pk: Blood-pressure-lowering effect develops over hours after oral dosing
Plasma concentrations peak roughly 2-4 hours after an oral dose
Elimination half-life approximately 5-6 hours, supporting once-daily dosing
Antihypertensive effect maintained over 24 hours with once-daily dosing
Store tablets at room temperature, protected from moisture, in the original container
pearls: Beta-1 selective with intrinsic beta-2 agonist and mild vasodilator activity - tends to have less bronchospasm and peripheral vasoconstriction than non-selective beta-blockers, but caution in airways disease still applies
Food markedly reduces absorption - dose before meals on an empty stomach and keep timing consistent
Do not withdraw abruptly - taper to avoid rebound hypertension, angina or arrhythmia
Not FDA-approved in the United States; dosing and indications based on EMA/SmPC and BNF
Avoid combining with IV verapamil/diltiazem due to risk of severe bradycardia and AV block
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue as usual. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, heart failure, AV block, bronchospasm and hypoglycaemia. Management is supportive: monitor ECG and blood pressure, give atropine for bradycardia, intravenous fluids and inotropes/vasopressors for hypotension, glucagon for refractory cardiac depression, and bronchodilators for bronchospasm; consider temporary pacing for severe block.
